newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIAN PRESIDENTIAL POLL OVERSHADOWED BY CRISIS.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIAN PRESIDENTIAL POLL OVERSHADOWED BY CRISIS.

text.p: Bulgarians vote on Sunday in presidential elections overshadowed by grave economic crisis and the killing three weeks ago of former prime minister Andrei Lukanov.
The president represents Bulgaria in its foreign relations but his duties are largely ceremonial and he lacks the power to intervene in the crisis triggered by the slow pace of structural reforms.

However the outcome of the election may be crucial for Prime Minister Zhan Videnov, whose position as Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP) leader has been shaken by his government's inability to deal with the crisis, analysts say.

"The main battle will begin after the presidential elections. For me the greatest challenge will be to get the BSP out of parliament," Ivan Kostov, leader of the opposition Union of Democratic Forces, told the daily Standard in an interview published on Thursday.

Polls show lawyer Petar Stoyanov, the candidate of the united opposition, ahead of his nearest rival, Socialist candidate and Culture Minister Ivan Marazov, but short of an absolute majority in the first round.
President Zhelyu Zhelev, 61, lost a U.S.-style primary to Stoyanov in June and is not standing for re-election. His relations with the Socialists have been frequently stormy.
Stoyanov says he would cooperate with any government trying to end the crisis but has raised the possibility of early parliamentary elections.
"If I win this election, there will be a new political situation in the country because this will be a vote against the BSP," he told a television debate on Tuesday.
Bulgaria has the lowest level of foreign investment of any country in the region and a quarter of its numerous and insolvent banks are in receivership.

The central bank is rapidly running out of money to prop up the lev and buy fuel and also wheat -- to replace Bulgarian production which was exported because the world price is higher than the local price.
Foreign exchange reserves fell to $506 million at end-September from $575 million in August and $1.47 billion in September 1995.

Economic indicators offer no glimmer of hope and Bulgaria risks becoming the first country to default on its Brady bonds, U.S. Treasury-backed paper which provides emerging economies with a mechanism for restructuring foreign debt burdens.
Inflation is forecast to exceed 200 percent this year and growth is expected to be negative. High interest rates introduced to stabilise the banking system have doubled internal debt.

An International Monetary Fund mission is due in Sofia next week to discuss a policy framework that would allow the fund to release a twice-delayed $115 million second tranche of funding under Bulgaria's standby accord.
Many Bulgarians say they have lost faith in the ability of politicians of any party to end the crisis and will not vote.
Violent crime is rising in line with poverty but colleagues say Lukanov's killing was political. The former premier was shot in front of his home on October 2 in an apparent contract killing.
A Socialist colleague of Lukanov, Andrei Raichev, said the former premier had been about to expose high-level corruption within the Socialist government when he was murdered.

"This was an act of political confrontation. I believe that whatever the motives were we should call it an act of political terrorism, and I hope it will be the last act of political violence," Socialist presidential candidate Marazov said.

A total of 13 pairs of presidential and vice-presidential candidates are contesting the election. If no candidate wins more than 50 percent of votes in the first round, a second round will be held a week later.
